title: Exploring concept creep: Youth's portrayal of ADHD on TikTok
screen_reason: Content analysis of 100 popular #ADHD TikTok videos in which every characteristic attributed to ADHD was coded for correspondence with an external ground truth (DSM-5-TR criteria). The paper reports quantitative shares with denominators for the non-corresponding (misinformation) share at claim level (225/411 = 55%), at video level (27/100 videos entirely misleading; 52/100 partial misinformation) and for behaviours attributed in the top comments (16/40 = 40%). The authors explicitly label the non-corresponding material misinformation/misleading, so this is a CONTENT prevalence study, not a detection, intervention or belief study.

estimates.country: Not stated (TikTok 'For You' page searched from the Netherlands; no country restriction on videos)
estimates.measure_type: % of characteristics attributed to ADHD in popular TikTok videos that did not align with the DSM-5-TR criteria for ADHD
estimates.denominator: 411 distinct characteristics that video creators attributed to ADHD across the 100 included TikTok videos
estimates.definition: A characteristic counted in the numerator if, after deductive coding against the DSM-5-TR criteria for ADHD (conservative approach: coded as DSM whenever interpretation allowed), it did not correspond with any of the 18 listed DSM-5-TR inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity criteria; such characteristics were then coded inductively into six categories of 'concept creep'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Our findings showed that 55 % of the characteristics that youth attributed to ADHD in their videos did not align with the DSM-5-TR criteria of this diagnosis"; the authors call this material misinformation: "Most videos (52 %) contained partial misinformation, while 27 % of them were entirely misleading."
estimates.source_quote: Video creators attributed a total of 411 distinct characteristics to ADHD in their videos. Of these, 186 (45 %) corresponded with the DSM- 5-TR criteria of ADHD, while 225 (55 %) did not.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The first two authors coded video transcripts deductively against the DSM-5-TR criteria for ADHD (APA, 2022) and inductively for non-DSM characteristics; 10 transcripts used to agree codes and decision rules, then 20 transcripts double-coded with 'good reliability (Kripendorff's binary kappa = 0.844, Cu-kappa = 0.795)'; the first author coded the remaining transcripts.
estimates.moderator_quote: TikTok’s ‘For You’ discovery page was searched on May 10, 2023 using the hashtag #ADHD. The search returned 24.7 billion hits. Videos on the ‘For you’-page are not presented chronologically, but rather based on an algorithm that takes into account the popularity of the videos, as well as the user’s location and viewing history ( Herrick et al., 2021 ). A new account was created for the search, to prevent previous engagement from influencing the results. The first 100 videos that met the inclusion criteria were collected. A video was included if it depicted behaviors or experiences which were attributed to ADHD. Videos were excluded if the estimated age of the creator was over 30, or if the creator mentioned any health care or research affiliations.
estimates.notes: borderline=true on the CONTENT-vs-QUALITY call: the numerator is non-correspondence with a diagnostic guideline rather than demonstrated falsity, and the authors' own discussion concedes that some incongruent characteristics (e.g. hyperfocus) are empirically associated with ADHD, so a defensible-but-true claim could land in the numerator. Coded CONTENT because items are judged one by one against an explicit external ground truth (DSM-5-TR) as aligned/not aligned and the paper itself reports the misaligned share as misinformation/misleading, with no multi-item quality instrument (no DISCERN/GQS/JAMA) involved. denom_scope=topical + denom_selection=curated because the corpus is a single-hashtag (#ADHD) set truncated to the first 100 algorithmically ranked (popular) videos. country coded Global: the sample is TikTok's global For You feed with no country filter; collection was run from the Netherlands and the algorithm takes account of user location, which the authors note.

estimates.country: Not stated (TikTok 'For You' page searched from the Netherlands; no country restriction on videos)
estimates.measure_type: % of popular #ADHD TikTok videos in which none of the depicted behaviours corresponded with the DSM-5-TR criteria (videos entirely misleading)
estimates.value_raw: 27/100 videos (27 %) entirely misleading; 52 partial misinformation; 21 wholly DSM-congruent
estimates.denominator: 100 popular TikTok videos attributing behaviours/experiences to ADHD (first 100 meeting inclusion criteria on the #ADHD 'For You' feed)
estimates.definition: A video counted in the numerator if none of the behaviours or experiences it attributed to ADHD corresponded with any DSM-5-TR criterion for ADHD; the authors describe these videos as 'entirely misleading'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Most videos (52 %) contained partial misinformation, while 27 % of them were entirely misleading."
estimates.source_quote: In only 21 of the 100 videos, all the mentioned characteristics corresponded with the DSM-5- TR criteria of ADHD. Most often (n = 52), creators mentioned a mix of DSM and non-DSM characteristics in their videos, while in 27 videos none of the behaviors corresponded with the DSM-5-TR criteria of ADHD.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same coding as the claim-level row: deductive coding of transcripts against DSM-5-TR criteria by the first two authors; 20 transcripts double-coded, Krippendorff's binary kappa = 0.844, Cu-kappa = 0.795.
estimates.moderator_quote: The first 100 videos that met the inclusion criteria were collected. A video was included if it depicted behaviors or experiences which were attributed to ADHD.
estimates.notes: Video-level counterpart of the claim-level 55 % row, hence definition_variant=true: this is the STRICTEST reading (videos with nothing DSM-congruent at all). The looser video-level reading the paper also states verbatim is 52 % 'partial misinformation'; the '79 % of videos contained at least some non-DSM characteristic' figure is a cross-category sum I computed and therefore did NOT keep (R8). Same CONTENT-vs-QUALITY caveat as the first row.

estimates.country: Not stated (TikTok 'For You' page searched from the Netherlands; no country restriction on videos)
estimates.measure_type: % of behaviours that top-commenters attributed to ADHD that did not match the DSM-5-TR criteria
estimates.denominator: 40 behaviours attributed to ADHD by commenters, within the 297 top comments (top three comments of each of the 100 videos, one video had comments disabled)
estimates.definition: A commenter-attributed behaviour counted in the numerator if it did not match any DSM-5-TR criterion for ADHD; coded the same way as the video characteristics.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Of the 40 behaviors that commenters attributed to ADHD, in total 24 (60 %) corresponded with the DSM-5-TR criteria" - the complement being behaviours outside the diagnostic criteria, which the paper treats as broadening/misinformation.
estimates.source_quote: Of the 40 behaviors that com - menters attributed to ADHD, in total 24 (60 %) corresponded with the DSM-5-TR criteria, of which 13 corresponded with the criteria of inat - tention and the other 11 with those of impulsivity-hyperactivity. Youth most frequently mentioned behavior that corresponded with criterion 1d: difficultly following through on instructions (n = 4) and criterion 2h: difficulty waiting your turn (n = 6). Of the 16 (40 %) behaviors that did not match the DSM-5-TR criteria, most (n = 12) overlapped with the incongruent behaviors mentioned in the videos
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Comments coded by the first two authors; a subset of 60 comments (from 20 videos) double-coded for the acceptance categories with Cu-kappa = 0.889; DSM correspondence of commenter-attributed behaviours coded with the same DSM-5-TR scheme as the videos.
estimates.moderator_quote: The top three comments from each of the 100 videos were also collected, resulting in a total of 297 comments (as the comment option was deactivated for one video). As with the videos, TikTok sorts the comments using an algorithm, which typically results in the comments with the most previous engagement appearing first. The most popular comments were selected, as their high engagement in terms of likes was seen as an indication that their content resonated with a large audience.
estimates.notes: Separate measure with its own denominator (comments, not videos), so a distinct row rather than a variant. Denominator is small (40 behaviours) and drawn only from the top three comments per video, which the authors flag as unrepresentative; confidence medium for that reason. The 40 % is stated verbatim, so R8 is satisfied. Same CONTENT-vs-QUALITY caveat as the other rows.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) the complement figures 45 % of characteristics and 21 % of videos DSM-congruent, and 60 % of commenter-attributed behaviours congruent - these are accuracy shares, the mirror of the rows already kept, so keeping them would double-count the same estimates; (b) 52 % of videos containing 'partial misinformation' - stated verbatim but it is the looser sibling of the 27 % row already kept in the same cell, and I kept one video-level point rather than two (R4); the 79 % sum (52+27) is a computed cross-category sum and is barred by R8. (c) The comment-reaction shares (59.6 % of commenters recognised the depicted behaviours in themselves; of the 118 who commented on the diagnostic claims, 55.1 % validated, 21.1 % accepted, 20.3 % rejected, 3.4 % questioned) are self-identification and acceptance of claims, not exposure to or prevalence of misinformation, so no row - belief/acceptance is explicitly out of scope. (d) The within-DSM split (75 % of the 186 congruent characteristics were inattention, 25 % hyperactivity-impulsivity) is a share computed inside the congruent (i.e. accurate) subset and measures nothing about misinformation prevalence. (e) Table 1 and Table 2 give per-behaviour video counts (e.g. 17/100 videos claiming 'feeling overwhelmed by thoughts'); these are sub-components of the same corpus and the instructions forbid inventing sub-rows from a pooled number, so they are left as texture. (f) The 8 % worldwide ADHD prevalence and the ~half-incorrect ADHD-information figure from Yeung et al. (2022)/Karasavva et al. (2025) are cited from elsewhere and barred by R8.

rob.design: Algorithmically ranked convenience sample: TikTok 'For You' page searched with #ADHD on 10 May 2023 from a newly created account (to null out personalisation); the first 100 videos meeting inclusion criteria retained, 11 excluded (creator estimated age >30, or health-care/research affiliation); views per video 37,200-19.3 million, 316.1 million views in total. Top three comments per video collected (297 comments; one video had comments disabled). Multimodal transcription (spoken audio, on-screen text, plus nonverbal/setting when relevant); no verbatim transcripts published for privacy (paraphrased/fictionalised examples instead). Coding: deductive against DSM-5-TR criteria plus inductive categories; first two authors agreed codes on 10 transcripts, double-coded 20 (Krippendorff's binary kappa = 0.844, Cu-kappa = 0.795), first author coded the remaining 80; comment categories double-coded on 60 comments (Cu-kappa = 0.889). No response rate applies (content study). Ethics approval PED-2223-S-0044, University of Groningen. Authors note the high reliability was reached only after extensive discussion and additional decision rules, which they concede may have introduced bias, and that findings may not generalise to less popular videos.
rob.item6_quote: First, we used deductive coding to identify behaviors that cor - responded with DSM-5-TR criteria of ADHD. A conservative approach was adopted, by coding behaviors using the DSM criteria whenever interpretation allowed.
rob.item10_quote: Video creators attributed a total of 411 distinct characteristics to ADHD in their videos. Of these, 186 (45 %) corresponded with the DSM- 5-TR criteria of ADHD, while 225 (55 %) did not.
